## Back

Less than a week ago, I found myself stimulating my brain to produce good feelings by exposing my eyeballs to some YouTube videos showing playthroughs of ZX Spectrum games. I found myself idly engaged by [a playthrough of Robin of the Woods](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vGIg5z7oE4w&t=672s), a game in which the player navigates a multiscreen medieval forest, nonchalantly clubbing enemies to crumbled unconsciousness for the crime of patrolling endlessly in straight lines.

This reminded me of, to my mind, a better ZX Spectrum game, Feud, about two wizards - brothers locked in bitter rivalry - who wander around a similar forested arena of largely black screens, seeking ingredients for potions which, when deposited at cauldrons near their bases, grant them spells which, ultimately, allow them to vanquish their sibling, thereby either losing the game (if the vanquished sibling is the player), or winning the game (if the vanquished sibling is the computer-controlled rival).

As [this video essay](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w7U8qCLbBUo) makes clear, in practice Feud probably isn't as good as I remember. Only a minority of spells matter, meaning only a minority of ingredients matter, meaning only a minority of locations matter. And as there's only one arena, which never changes, after a few playthroughs beating the game becomes just a matter of repeating the same routes, acquiring the same ingredients, shooting fire and lightning into the rival until he, Wicked Witch of the West Style, descends into the floor, producing a single perfunctory "Victory" screen.

But the core loop - search, collect, upgrade, repeat; all while competing against a rival trying to do the same - along with the highly distinct visual 'style' of the ZX Spectrum, made me think maybe there's something worth pulling out of misremembered nostalgia and making real in the present day. And it made me think of the Home Computer systems I had during the 1980s through to mid 1990s, and how the types of game, and experience of gaming, changed with each system.

From this, the kernel of a game idea, Upgrade, was born. And with Claude Fable, in the Claude Code scaffold, it turned out this game idea was relatively straightforward to conjur into some form of existence. And then, more promisingly, to iterate upon and tune through more than a dozen rounds of playtesting and feature development.

# Up: The Upgrade Game

**Play it: [jonminton.github.io/upgrade-game](https://jonminton.github.io/upgrade-game/)** · [map editor](https://jonminton.github.io/upgrade-game/editor.html) · [source](https://github.com/JonMinton/upgrade-game)

## The core loop

The core conceit is that the upgrades don't make your character stronger. They make the *game* better.

Every entity in the world - you, your rival, the environment - has a development tier. The tier controls only presentation: resolution, palette, colour rules, animation smoothness, sound hardware. Movement speed, attack power and health are identical at every tier. What you are racing for is not power. It is fidelity.

The loop wrapped around that conceit is Feud's, transplanted. You navigate a flick-screen arena - a British-folklore valley of village, greenwood, marsh and ruined keep - looking for shards: relics of future hardware half-buried in the landscape, a thermionic valve glowing among the reeds, a 3.5" floppy stuck in a tree like the sword in the stone. Gather three, carry them to the Standing Stones, and survive a three-second channelling ritual - interruptible, naturally, by anyone minded to shoot you mid-chant - and the whole game re-renders underneath you, one tier closer to 1995.

You are not the only one foraging. Kernagh, a rival hedge-wizard, starts at the same tier as you but on the far side of the valley, and wants exactly what you want. Combat is kept simple: one projectile, a crackling static bolt; three hits and you are derezzed - dissolved into a burst of noise pixels, dropping every shard you were carrying where you fell, respawning at your home village one tier lower than you were. And there are two ways to win: transcendence, in which you reach the top tier, gather three final shards, and complete one last, longer ritual before Kernagh does; or elimination, in which you derez him while he is already scraping along the floor at T0. Each, of course, has its mirror image, in which the wizard transcended against, or derezzed at rock bottom, is the player, and the game is thereby lost rather than won.

The rule that makes the race legible - and, I think, the best idea in the game - is this: the *environment* renders at your tier, but each *avatar* renders at its own. The world is your game; the rival is a visitor from his. So a silky sixteen-colour sprite gliding through your attribute-clashing Spectrum forest tells you instantly - and unsettlingly - that Kernagh is ahead. It works on the ear as well as the eye: his footsteps and zaps bleed through from adjacent screens at *his* tier's sound quality. Beeper clicks while he trails you; increasingly rich stereo samples as he pulls away.

## Attribute clash, and why it existed

The Spectrum had a very distinctive graphical style, and it was a style produced entirely by a limitation. The machine let you specify pixels as 'on' or 'off' at a comparatively high resolution - but the *colours* associated with 'on' and 'off' could only be specified for 8×8 tiles of cells within that resolution.

This wasn't an oversight. The Spectrum wasn't really designed with games in mind; it was designed for more serious applications. Consider a simple word processor: a letter is a block of pixels that fits neatly inside one of those colour tiles. Being able to change the complete foreground and background colour of that block at once is exactly what you want for marking out letters for attention, editing, highlighting. Higher-resolution colour control - making the *edges* of a letter a different colour from its interior - would have bought you almost nothing.

So the constraint was rational, and the consequence was an entire visual idiom: the colour bleed as a sprite crosses a tile boundary, the careful level design that works *with* the grid rather than against it. A generation of British game artists spent a decade learning to make attribute clash look deliberate.

## The tier ladder

| Tier | Machine modelled | What changes |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **T0** | Late-70s / ZX81-ish | 1-bit monochrome, chunky glyphs, near-silence. The floor - you can't fall below it. |
| **T1** | ZX Spectrum 48K | 256×192, 8×8 attribute cells, full clash faithfully modelled. 1-channel beeper. **Player start.** |
| **T2** | Spectrum 128 / Amstrad-ish | Clash minimised by smarter cell alignment. AY chip: 3 channels, music and SFX coexist. |
| **T3** | C64-style 8-bit | 16 fixed colours, hardware sprites free of the attribute grid, push-scroll instead of screen-flick. SID-ish sound. |
| **T4** | Atari ST / EGA | 16 from 512, 8-frame animation, doubled tile detail. Sampled drums. |
| **T5** | Amiga | 32+ colours, parallax, anti-aliased sprites, ambient animation. 4-channel MOD music. **Win tier.** |

My own rungs on this ladder: ZX Spectrum 48K; ZX Spectrum 128K; Amiga 500; Amiga 1200. Then, eventually, PCs - but that's a different story and a duller one.

> **\[TODO\]** The machines list is the personal spine of the section and it's currently four nouns. Worth expanding: which of these machines was *yours* versus the household's, roughly when each arrived, and what the jump between each one felt like at the time. The Spectrum→Amiga gap is the emotional engine of the game's core mechanic.

T1 is where you start, because the Spectrum is where *I* started. T0 exists as a floor: true monochrome purgatory, the place you fall to and the place you can be eliminated from. T3 and T4 - the C64 and the Atari ST - were never part of my own history, but they're the obvious intermediate rungs on the way to the Amiga.

Though I'll admit that putting the ST *below* the Amiga rather than beside it reflects a set of loyalties formed around 1990 and never seriously re-examined.

Three things in that image are worth slowing down for.

The **shard** changes medium as you climb: a cassette tape at the Spectrum tiers, a 3.5" floppy at the C64 and ST, a CD at the Amiga. You are always collecting the storage format of the era you can currently perceive.

The **wizard-on-grass** row is the attribute rule made visible. There are two identical trees in that cell, one either side of him. Up to T1, the tree sharing his 8×8 cell is forced to *his* colour while its twin, one cell over, stays green. From T2 the sprite carries its own colours and both trees are left alone. That is the whole of the previous section in a single 32-pixel square.

And the **walk cycle** gets longer as you climb - one pose, two, four, four, six, six. I didn't decide that. The generator samples the animation and de-duplicates on pixel content, so those counts are whatever the renderers actually produce.[^1]

[^1]: **Claude Footnote:** The generator lives at `/assets.html` in the repo and never draws an asset itself - every cell is cropped out of a real `renderPlay()` pass over a synthetic world, so the sheet can't drift from the game. Worth noting how easily this kind of derivation goes wrong: the first version sampled 48 units of animation distance and confidently reported four poses at T4. The walk frame and the sine bob above T3 only drift through each other by a distance of about 60, so two of the six poses simply never appeared in the window. The count looked plausible, which is exactly what made it dangerous.

## Wands, berries and other refinements

More than a dozen playtest rounds turned that single loop into something with texture. Two of the additions matter enough to describe.

**The wands.** The first prototypes had one weapon. Now a pedestal in your home village lets you swap the default firewand - a point of damage and a brief stagger - for an icewand, which does no damage at all but freezes its target for three and a half seconds. The trade-off is real. The firewand is the attrition route: it is how tiers get knocked off Kernagh, and a derezzed wizard scatters his carried shards where he falls, ready for looting. The icewand harms nobody, and instead wins tempo: three and a half seconds is long enough to complete your own ritual while your rival stands frozen beside the stones, or to walk off with the shards he was guarding. Damage the rival, in other words, or merely inconvenience him at precisely the right moment.

**The berries.** Bushes scattered across the valley - densest in the greenwood - heal one heart when walked over, and regrow after thirty seconds or so. Kernagh knows about them too, and goes foraging when hurt - which turns his retreats into information: a wounded rival heads for woodland.

## The arena: drawn, then grown

The arena went through three regimes: hand-shaped, then editable, then grown.

The editor came first, and it made the map a thing to iterate on rather than a thing to commit to: paint tiles on any screen, preview them at any tier through the game's *real* renderers, check connectivity, and apply the result to the live game. Maps became shareable JSON files, and contributed maps now land in the repo as pull requests.

Then the map generator, which grows features from rules rather than stamping down templates. Rivers flow edge to edge with momentum and meander, and usually fork a tributary. Forests grow as blob clusters; reeds colonise the riverbanks. Berries are placed by weighted acceptance - roughly ten times likelier where two or more trees stand within a couple of tiles - so they concentrate in woodland without ever being told to. The stone circle repels both wizards' bases; the bases repel each other; shrines scatter themselves at polite distances from everything of importance.

But the real lesson of the generator is that a generated map is not automatically a *playable* one, and most of its apparent cleverness is really a cascade of checks and repairs. Bridges are added only where they measurably reconnect a genuinely unreachable region - and where the blockage is trees rather than water, a "villager clearing" is carved through the thinnest point instead, as if the locals had opened the way. A final repair pass proves every shrine, the altar and both homes reachable, and carves an emergency path if not. Procedural generation, it turns out, is mostly not generation. It is validation.

The shipped default map, GLEN, is itself grown - but from a hand-picked seed, chosen by scanning a hundred candidates for the qualities the original hand-made map had been designed around: village and keep far apart, a full-width meandering river bridged in exactly two places, a riverbank ruin near the village. And GLEN is fixed across all games, deliberately, so that it can be learned. Variety lives elsewhere (next section); GLEN is for mastery - familiarity paying off exactly as it did in Feud.

> **\[TODO\]** Your notes call the generation rules "CA style" - the ruin-weathering rule is cellular-automaton-like, but the feature generator is closer to rule-based growth than a classic CA. Adjust the terminology to taste. A screenshot of a rejected or mid-repair map would also earn its place here, if one can be captured.

## Reasons to go back in

Two kinds of incentive persist between games: what the game unlocks, and what the valley remembers.

**The unlocks.** Games start in easy mode, with Kernagh degraded only at the decision level - short-sighted, slow to re-plan, prone to holding his fire - while his movement speed, and every rule of the game, stay identical to yours. Win, and the victory screen concedes "BUT THIS WAS THE EASY SIGNAL...", offering to continue directly into hard mode, where the full AI is waiting. That first easy win also permanently unlocks two title-screen options: hard mode, and seeded chaos. Chaos mode generates a fresh valley every game and announces its seed, so that a good valley can be shared; seeded chaos lets you type in a friend's seed and play their exact world. And the Hall of Signals - a top-eight, arcade-initials score table, hard-mode scores doubled, every entry tagged with the map it was set on - gives all of this somewhere to accumulate.

**The scars.** The arena deforms under combat. A firebolt that dies against a tree occasionally ignites it: the tree burns - animated at every tier - sometimes spreads to its neighbours, and collapses into a solid burnt stump. An icebolt that dies against a standing stone occasionally frost-splits it into cracked rock. And these scars *persist*: each map keeps a damage ledger, and every completed game weathers that ledger once. Stumps mostly remain, sometimes decay to bare earth, and occasionally resolve into a pushstone - a boulder that can then be hauled, at a fraction of walking speed and considerable effort, to somewhere tactically useful. Play GLEN for a week and your GLEN slowly stops being anyone else's: thinned where your battles happened, its geography quietly rewritten by your own history of bad decisions.

And the valley's slow evolution has an end state. The arena border is only trees, and trees burn. If a border stump decays away between games, the world develops a hole; step through it and you find The Void - nothing to see, nothing to do, the conflict is over. No score. No hall entry. The valley's entire history resets to genesis.

# Across: Opus 5, Fable 5, and two ways of being good

The second act is about performance - the game's, and then the models'.

## The slowdown

Somewhere around T3, games started to bog down. Not immediately: the slowdown accumulated over a session, which is the worst kind, because it means the problem isn't a single expensive operation but something leaking.

> **\[TODO\]** Describe the symptom concretely before diagnosing it. What did it actually feel like at T3, ten minutes in? Frame rate? Input lag? This is what motivates the whole investigation and it's currently one clause in the notes.

Three models looked at it, in sequence, and - this turned out to matter - not blind to each other.

**GPT**, via GitHub Copilot, went first, and identified a set of issues likely to be responsible.

**Gemini**, via Gemini Code Assist, went second. It could see GPT's review, and judged it better than its own.

**Opus 5**, via Claude Code, went third. It drew its inspiration mainly from GPT - specifically from GPT's instinct to evaluate performance under different conditions - and then took that much further than GPT had, running many experiments directly in the codebase. It confirmed that the GPT-identified problems were substantive, but found that the *order of priority* was different from what GPT had assumed: the things GPT thought mattered most for latency weren't the things that actually did.

**Fable** then read the resulting review reports and implemented the changes largely as the panel had recommended.

The non-blindness is the interesting part. This wasn't three independent opinions to be averaged. It was a relay, in which each model could see and build on what came before - and in Gemini's case, defer to it. Which means the panel's output isn't a consensus so much as an accumulation, and GPT's framing had disproportionate influence on everything downstream simply by going first.

> **\[TODO\]** Worth deciding whether the relay structure was a deliberate choice or just how it happened. If deliberate, say why; if accidental, the observation about first-mover influence is worth keeping as a caution about how to run these panels.

## Swot and Savant

Within recent LLM performance benchmarks, Opus 5 - despite being nominally a tier below Fable 5, and at half the cost per token[^2] - achieves similar performance on many technical and applied-knowledge tasks.

[^2]: **Claude Footnote:** The per-token figures at time of writing: Claude Fable 5 is \$10 per million input tokens and \$50 per million output; Claude Opus 5 is \$5 and \$25. So "half the cost per token" is exactly right, on both input and output.

I don't have a strong reason to doubt this, beyond the usual worry about which metrics got chosen. But my initial impression is that the two models often reach similar outcomes by quite different routes. Crudely: Opus 5 is more of a **swot**, and Fable 5 more of a **savant**.

**Swot behaviour:**

- Even more extensive and comprehensive RAG searches
- Even more comprehensive review of codebases
- Even more exhaustive testing and iteration

**Savant behaviour:**

- More reliance on reasoning from first principles
- More creative, and often more intelligent, inference about the latent subgoals and implicit assumptions behind a prompt

Both have very high tenacity - though I suspect that's a dial being turned in response to capacity and demand rather than a fixed property of either model.

> **\[TODO - Scriptdoctor\]** "Swot" and "Savant" is a good pairing but the swot list is currently three lines all beginning "Even more". Either lean into the repetition as a deliberate rhythm or vary it. Flagging rather than fixing.

> **\[TODO\]** Give one concrete instance of each behaviour from the actual Upgrade work. The distinction is doing a lot of load-bearing work in this post and right now it's asserted rather than demonstrated. The performance investigation should supply both: Opus running many experiments (swot), Fable reading the reports and inferring what you actually wanted from them (savant).

## Why Fable *shouldn't* be more swottish

So although Opus 5 and Fable 5 are intended as different tiers, for now they can perhaps be thought of as similarly capable models that often reach similar outcomes by different means.

And there's a reason Fable probably *shouldn't* try to be more swottish. Its guardrails hair-trigger whenever anything touching biology or cybersecurity happens to be searched for or reasoned about.[^3] The more exhaustively it searched and explored, the more likely it would be to trip one of those by chance. Given that its token cost is double Opus 5's, it shouldn't go too far in that direction in any case.

[^3]: **Claude Footnote:** Concretely, Fable 5 can decline a request by returning a normal response with a `refusal` stop reason and a category - `bio` and `cyber` among them - rather than an error. Anthropic's own guidance is that benign adjacent work in security tooling and the life sciences can trip these as false positives, which is why the API offers a server-side fallback to another model. Worth noting for the argument here: Opus 5 also ships with elevated cybersecurity safeguards, so the difference between the two is one of degree rather than kind. Jon - you may want to soften the claim above accordingly, or leave it as your impression and let this footnote do the qualifying.

Two implications follow.

**Fable and Opus should, for now, be considered complementary siblings** rather than rungs on a ladder.

**And "half the cost per token" is not "half the cost per project."** Because of its swottishness, Opus 5 burns more tokens than Fable in search and evaluation - which erodes the advantage of the model that looks twice as cheap.

That was a guess when I first wrote it down. It turns out it has already been measured, and it is worth being precise about what the measurement does and doesn't support.

On Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, at max effort, Opus 5 scores 61 and Fable 5 scores 60 - a tie, for practical purposes. Getting there took Opus 5 **100 million output tokens** against Fable's **87 million**: about 15% more output to reach the same place, and enough to earn Opus the label *very verbose* where Fable is only *somewhat verbose*. Running the whole suite cost \$3,835 on Opus against \$5,630 on Fable.

So the direction of the hunch is right, and the mechanism is right. But the magnitude isn't: half price per token becomes roughly **26–32% cheaper per completed task**, not parity.[^4] The swottishness eats about half of Opus's price advantage. It doesn't eat all of it.

[^4]: **Claude Footnote:** Two different published figures, same conclusion. Artificial Analysis's weighted cost per Index task is \$2.03 for Opus 5 against \$2.75 for Fable 5 (26% lower); total evaluation cost across the suite gives 32% lower. Both are a long way from the 50% the sticker price implies.

I've put the full arithmetic - including why output tokens alone don't quite account for the gap, and the one measurement that points the other way - in a companion post: [The token tax: what "half the price" actually buys](../opus-fable-cost-per-task/index.qmd).

Anyway: the agentic circular firing squad - asking one LLM to try to rip apart another's codebase, then another, then implementing what survives - worked well for identifying and fixing the performance issues, and Opus 5 was a critical part of that mix.

# Down: The pushback

## What happened

I posted Upgrade to the show-and-tell channel of a local game-development community, some of whose members I'd recently met in person.

The first response was warm: "very cool idea!". I replied that the game had been through about fourteen rounds of development, including some attempts at optimising performance, and that there were some unadvertised behaviours and features that would hopefully reward replay. This drew more warmth still - "oh wow, that's committed" - together with a question about playtesting, and a self-reflection from the same person about their own past habit of making things in a trance, pushing them out, and being done with them.

Then a second person added, with a smiley, that they assumed it takes rather less commitment if you're just asking Claude to do it.

I hadn't tried to hide the collaboration, and said so:

> Clue's in the git log and pseudonym. 😉 I meant mainly in terms of game behaviour, dynamics, balance, features, the progression loop etc. for example introduced a means of procedurally generating the maps to produce more organic rivers and forests, then specifying and implementing cellular automata style rules for how they change between visits. But also noticed performance issues creeping in and used a kind of agentic circular firing squad (asking one LLM to try to rip apart another's codebases etc) to try to fix this.
>
> There is an editor through the /editor/ path off root. So means of providing more human input to assets.

A few hours later, the first person returned: they hadn't realised the game was made with AI. They didn't want to restart a conversation the community had evidently had before. But as someone who tries to check out, and reply to, as much of what gets posted there as they can, they were starting to feel discouraged from doing so by the absence of an AI disclosure rule. They would rather know in advance, and just not interact. They raised it with the moderators - politely, and explicitly heading off any pile-on - and their message drew more hearts than anything else in the thread, including my game. A moderator thanked them, and said the question was already under active discussion.

Two things seem worth being honest about here.

First, "I hadn't tried to hide it" is true, but it isn't the whole truth. The name credited is Jon Fableton. The public repo lists Claude as a collaborator throughout. The clue was, as I said at the time, in the git log and the pseudonym. But a clue is not a declaration. The disclosure was discoverable rather than upfront - and the person who asked for a rule had engaged twice, generously, without discovering it. Their request, boiled down, was that the gap between discoverable and upfront be closed.

Second, nobody was hostile. The joke wore a wink. The request was courteous, framed around the requester's own finite attention rather than around my conduct; and the hearts it gathered were support for *disclosure*, not a movement against me. If this was pushback, it was the mildest weather system to which that word has ever been applied.

And yet it stung, and it is worth working out exactly what stung, because it wasn't an accusation. Nobody said the game was bad, or that I had done anything wrong. What the exchange did was quietly reprice the work: fourteen rounds of development read as commitment right up until the moment its co-author was named, whereupon - to at least one reader - it read as none at all.

## Where the commitment lives

The joke's premise deserves to be taken seriously, because it is doing real work. A show-and-tell channel doesn't only trade in artifacts; it trades in evidence of effort. "That's committed" was praise for the fourteen rounds. "Less commitment if you're just asking Claude" was the claim that those rounds don't count - that commitment lives at the keyboard, in the typing of the code, and nowhere else.

My reply, in effect, relocated it: the commitment was in game behaviour, dynamics, balance, features, the progression loop - in the several hundred decisions about what the game should be, which of its emergent behaviours to keep, and what each playtest's irritations actually meant. Claude typed nearly every line. The design ledger is mine. Whether that ledger counts as commitment is, I suspect, exactly the question the next few years of this argument will be about.

To earn its place here it probably needs just two concrete examples: one design decision that was unambiguously yours, and one thing Claude originated that you chose to keep. Verify "Claude typed nearly every line" while you're at it.

## The false binary

The request was for advance declaration of AI-coproduced content, so that those who wished to could disengage before spending attention rather than after. The framing underneath it is that a work either is or is not AI-coproduced - and that the line can be drawn cleanly enough for a moderator to enforce.

It can't. Nothing is ever fully AI or fully human. There is always some mixture, and the range of possible mixtures is very wide: AI engagement with human content, human engagement with AI content, and every ratio in between. I'm still learning where the right balance sits, and so is everyone else. Cognitive centaurs.[^5]

## Which way the tide runs

Workflows with AI *will* come to outcompete workflows without AI across pretty much every dimension, and will become the dominant means of doing games development - or any other kind of analytical, technical, systems work - within one to five years.

When that happens, the falseness of the binary will be generally recognised. During the transition, though, there will be groups and cliques that increasingly define themselves by their opposition to AI. To the extent that some consumers share those sentiments, those groups may get short-term bumps in engagement and support.

But these are ripples running against the direction of the main tide.

## Multiplier, not replacement

At its best, AI is a multiplier for human knowledge, curiosity and creativity - not a replacement for them. It already lets hunches, eddies and asides be developed into full-blown prototypes faster and more cheaply than ever before, which makes it far easier to work out whether the hunches were worth having.

Upgrade is itself an instance of this. It began as a hunch about the ZX Spectrum's colour limitations being a game mechanic rather than a constraint. Under the old economics, that hunch would have stayed a hunch.

Creative and curious people won't run out of creativity and curiosity. The collapse in implementation cost means new demand will emerge to meet the new supply: Jevons' effect.

## The Lump of Labour

This is the corrective to the intuitive framing of AI's role, and it explains why AI is so often instinctively seen as a threat. The instinct is the **Lump of Labour fallacy**: the assumption that there is a fixed, finite demand for stuff - prototypes, games, analytic outputs, websites, databases, papers - so that any technology reducing the cost of producing that stuff must reduce the total labour an industry can support, and therefore put people out of work.

The irony is that some of the less insightful *proponents* of AI in business - mid and senior managers, executives - subscribe to exactly the same fallacy. They are attracted to implementing AI for precisely the reason many other people are repelled by it: they think they can and should simply reduce headcount.

And there's a sting in that.

Large organisations tend to be *less* adaptable to the pace of change required to get the best out of AI. They have standards, procedures, conventions and long-established ways of working that will ultimately impede the wholesale reconfiguration of work, tasks and roles that would let them use AI to multiply what their employees can do. Smaller, nimbler, AI-native organisations - without the cold hand of history and path dependency - can structure themselves from scratch around agentic working, and will very soon be able to outcompete the old behemoths.

Which produces the beautiful outcome: if a large, slowly-adapting organisation *does* use AI to justify making talented staff redundant en masse, those former staff are now better placed than ever before to form AI-native startups and destroy their alma maters.

But only if the laid-off staff recognise that AI is the solution rather than the problem, and embrace it as a multiplier of human effort rather than rejecting and opposing it.

## The long arc

AI is ultimately 'just' another instance of a decades-long tendency in the applied information sciences, which has progressed along two axes:

1.  Information retrieval, production and processing speeds increase.
2.  The level of abstraction and generalisation at which humans instruct machines goes *up* - becoming more about intent and outcome, and less about process and mechanism.

Examples of the second axis include pretty much any programming language above machine code and assembly - anything that uses human-like nouns and verbs. Including the BASIC that shipped with every ZX Spectrum.

AI differs in two ways, though. First in the breadth and pace at which things are changing. And second in potentially reducing the premium for specialisation as against generalism.
